title: Irony vs. Cover-up? Facial Dynamics of Positive Utterances in Negative Contexts in Japanese Speakers
abstract: Abstract The present study examined how Japanese speakers express verbal irony through prosody and dynamic facial behavior. Native Japanese speakers performed short-scripted dialogues that ended with the same positive utterance with positive (sincere) or negative intentional contexts. The speaker’s intent in the negative context was further classified, based on post-recording interviews, as irony or a socially smoothing “cover-up” stance. We extracted prosodic features (utterance duration, fundamental frequency, and intensity) and facial features (frame-by-frame facial action units and gaze direction). Prosodic measures primarily distinguished sincere productions from negative-context stances,with sincere productions showing higher pitch and greater intensity; irony productions were longer than their corresponding sincere productions. Facial measures revealed clearer differences among the production groups. Irony was associated with sustained brow-related activity and enhanced mouth-opening activity, together with an early downward-right gaze tendency. Sincere utterances showed stronger smile-related activity and a tendency toward upward-right gaze, whereas cover-up had an intermediate and heterogeneous profile. These findings provide a time-resolved account of multimodal stance marking in Japanese and suggest that positive utterances in negative situations may reflect not only ironic intent but also socially smoothing speaker intentions.
